title: Famous laws of software
note: The eponymous laws are compressed experience, not physics. Conway's and Brooks's laws are about people, Hyrum's and Postel's about interfaces, Amdahl's about parallel speedup, and Hofstadter's and Goodhart's about estimates and metrics. Know the exact wording, and know when each one applies.

read.title: Laws about people, interfaces, and limits
text: Some of the best-known laws in software are really about people. In 1968 Melvin Conway observed that organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structures: three teams tend to build a three-part system. Fred Brooks, reflecting on IBM's OS/360 in The Mythical Man-Month, added that putting more people on a late project makes it later, because newcomers must be trained and every extra person multiplies the lines of communication.

Others are about interfaces. Jon Postel's robustness principle, from an early TCP specification, advises being conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept. Hyrum's law is the warning that comes with it: once an API has enough users, someone will depend on every behavior they can observe, documented or not, so even a harmless change can break a client.

Amdahl's law sets a hard limit on parallelism. If 5 percent of a program must run serially, no number of processors can make it more than 20 times faster. Finally, Goodhart's law guards against bad metrics: count lines of code or closed tickets as a goal, and people will produce lines and tickets rather than value.
